studies.title: Efficacy and Safety of Co-Administered St. John's Wort and Ginkgo biloba Extracts in Patients with Subjective Tinnitus: A Preliminary Prospective Randomi
studies.abstract: It is widely accepted that extracts of St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) improve depressive symptoms, and tinnitus patients commonly presented with either mild depression or anxiety. We investigated whether co-administration of St. John's wort and Ginkgo biloba extracts can suppress tinnitus. Participants with subjective tinnitus aged 30-70 years were randomly assigned to the experimental (co-administration of St. John's wort and Ginkgo biloba extract; n = 20) or control (Ginkgo biloba extract only; n = 26) group for 12 weeks. Participants were blinded to the group assignments. After 12 weeks of treatment, no significant change in the minimum masking level on the tinnitogram was observed in either group. In the co-administration group, the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) score decreased from 34.7 (SD, 15.9) to 29.6 (16.0) (p = 0.102). However, the control group showed a significant decrease in THI score, from 30.5 (16.7) to 25.6 (17.1) (p = 0.046). Regarding the Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36), only the "Social Functioning" domain score changed significantly after extract co-administration, from 74.5 (21.5) to 83.9 (20.5) (p = 0.047). Co-administration of St. John's wort and Ginkgo biloba extracts did not improve the symptoms of subjective tinnitus compared to administration of Ginkgo biloba extract alone.

studies.title: St. John's wort versus placebo in social phobia: results from a placebo-controlled pilot study.
studies.abstract: Recognition of social anxiety disorder (social phobia) as a common and disabling condition has led to new advances in its pharmacotherapy. Limitations with selective seroton reuptake inhibitors (side effects) and behavior therapy (scarcity of trained therapists), coupled with the tendency for patients with the disorder to self-medicate with alternative treatments, have led to the interest in Saint John's wort (SJW) (Hypericum perforatum) for this disorder. Although the literature is mixed, SJW has demonstrated efficacy in several double-blind depression trials, and some open-label studies with anxiety disorders. There is pharmacokinetic evidence for the serotonergic, domaminergic, and GABAminergic activity of hypericum, all of which are implicated in social anxiety disorder. This study was designed to generate pilot data to examine the potential efficacy of SJW in generalized social anxiety disorder. Forty subjects were randomized to 12 weeks of treatment with a flexible dose (600-1800 mg) of SJW (n = 20) or placebo (n = 20). Subjects with comorbid depression (clinician HAMD > 16) were excluded. Results found no significant difference between mean change on the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale with SJW (11.4) and placebo (13.2), P = 0.27, effect size = -0.09. Post-hoc analyses found larger effects sizes associated with increased baseline severity, omitting patients with variable scores (+/-30%) during the first week, and use of self-report HAMD scores for exclusion. Results of the study fail to provide evidence for the efficacy of SJW in social phobia. The impact of methodologic improvements on signal detection, while suggestive of improvement, remains to be established.

studies.title: The effectiveness of St. John's Wort in major depressive disorder: a naturalistic phase 2 follow-up in which nonresponders were provided alternate medication.
studies.abstract: A continuation study of an extract of St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) for depression was performed in follow-up to an acute study that found no significant difference between St. John's wort extract and placebo. Seventeen subjects with DSM-IV-defined major depressive disorder who responded to St. John's wort extract in the acute-phase study (phase 1) were continued on double-blind treatment with the same preparation for 24 weeks. Ninety-five subjects who did not respond to either St. John's wort or placebo were treated with an antidepressant for 24 weeks. During antidepressant treatment, mean scores on the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression for phase 1 nonresponders decreased significantly (p <.0001), with no significant difference between St. John's wort nonresponders and placebo nonresponders. Of the 17 subjects continued on treatment with St. John's wort extract, 5 (29.4%) relapsed. The subjects who did not respond to St. John's wort extract or placebo in phase 1 were, by and large, not resistant to antidepressant treatment. This suggests that the lack of efficacy found by Shelton et al. in the acute-phase study was unlikely to be the result of a high proportion of treatment-resistant subjects.

studies.title: St. John's wort in mild to moderate depression: the relevance of hyperforin for the clinical efficacy.
studies.abstract: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter study, the clinical efficacy and safety of two different extracts of St. John's wort were investigated in 147 male and female outpatients suffering from mild or moderate depression according to DSM-IV criteria. Following a placebo run-in period of three to seven days, the patients were randomized to one of three treatment groups: During the 42-day treatment period, they received 3 x 1 tablets of either placebo, Hypericum extract WS 5573 (300 mg, with a content of 0.5% hyperforin), or Hypericum extract WS 5572 (300 mg, with a content of 5% hyperforin). The manufacturing process for the two Hypericum preparations was identical, so that they differed only in their hyperforin content. Efficacy regarding depressive symptoms was assessed on days 0, 7, 14, 28, and 42, using the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAMD, 17-item version) and the Depression Self-Rating Scale (D-S) according to von Zerssen. In addition, the severity of illness was also rated by the investigators on days 0 and 42 using the Clinical Global Impression (CGI) scale. The last observation of patients withdrawn from the trial prematurely was carried forward. At the end of the treatment period (day 42), the patients receiving WS 5572 (5% hyperforin) exhibited the largest HAMD reduction versus day 0 (10.3 +/- 4.6 points; mean +/- SD), followed by the WS 5573 group (0.5% hyperforin; HAMD reduction 8.5 +/- 6.1 points) and the placebo group (7.9 +/- 5.2 points). As regards the change in the HAMD total score between day 0 and treatment end and its relationship to the hyperforin dose, a significant monotonic trend was demonstrated in the Jonckheere-Terpstra test (p = 0.017). In pairwise comparisons, WS 5572 (5% hyperforin) was superior to placebo in alleviating depressive symptoms according to HAMD reduction (Mann-Whitney U-test: p = 0.004), whereas the clinical effects of WS 5573 (0.5% hyperforin) and placebo were descriptively comparable. These results show that the therapeutic effect of St. John's Wort in mild to moderate depression depends on its hyperforin content.

studies.title: St. John's Wort-Induced Supraventricular Tachycardia.
studies.abstract: St. John's wort, a non-FDA-approved over-the-counter (OTC) herbal supplement with antidepressant activity known as Hypericum perforatum, has been found to induce supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) in the absence of any underlying structural cardiac abnormality or known medical history via currently unclear pathophysiology. In this case presentation, the authors present a case of a 33-year-old female who presented with recurrent episodes of palpitations one month after initiating St. John's wort for the treatment of depression, which ultimately resolved upon cessation of the herbal supplement. Therefore, the postulated insinuating event is suspected to be the ingestion of St. John's wort. This will be the first documented case of St. John's wort-induced SVT. This case study brings into question the safety of the use of this agent as an OTC supplement for the management of depression. Further investigation is required to aid in the knowledge and understanding of the causative mechanism and to identify those patients who are at potentially heightened risks of such manifestations.

studies.title: Bidirectional interactions between St. John´s wort and gut microbiome: Potential implications on gut-brain-axis.
studies.abstract: Emerging evidence highlights the role of gut microbiome in mental health disorders, including depression, raising the question whether the action of antidepressants could be mediated, at least in part, via the microbiome-gut-brain axis. To explore this, we subjected a St. John's wort extract (STW 3-VI), clinically proven to be effective in mild to moderate depression, to a model of the upper and lower intestinal tract, including static in vitro predigestion followed by ex vivo incubation with human microbiota samples. To cover the interindividual diversity of gut microbiome composition, fecal samples from ten healthy volunteers were used. Although unchanged levels of most annotated compounds were observed during simulated upper intestinal tract digestion, incubation with fecal microbiota led to a significant change of the chemical profile of the extract. While hyperforins remained stable, flavonoids and hypericins were rapidly biotransformed, suggesting that they may act as prodrugs. Several metabolites were formed, many of which are known to be involved in gut-brain communication. Differential abundance analysis revealed significant changes in microbiome composition, particularly for taxa known to be potentially associated with depression. Among others, the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio, known to be lowered in depressive patients, was increased. Functional profiling revealed modulation of pathways involved in gut-brain communication, such as tyrosine and tryptophan metabolism. These bidirectional interactions suggest for the first time the gut microbiome as a potential mediator of the pharmacological effects of St. John's wort extracts via the microbiome-gut-brain axis.

studies.title: Evaluating the safety of St. John's Wort in human pregnancy.
studies.abstract: St. John's Wort is a herbal therapy, shown to be effective in treating mild to moderate depression; a disease common in women in their childbearing years. With a significant proportion of unplanned pregnancies, exposure to St. John's Wort into pregnancy is expected to occur. The purpose of this study was to determine whether exposure to this agent in pregnancy is associated with major malformations. We prospectively collected and followed subjects taking St. John's Wort and compared them to a matched group of pregnant women taking other pharmacologic therapy for depression and a third group of healthy women, not exposed to any known teratogens. We obtained follow-up information on 54 St. John's Wort exposed pregnancies and 108 pregnancies in the two comparator groups. Our results indicated that the rates of major malformations were similar across the three groups, with 5%, 4% and 0% in the St. John's Wort, disease comparator, and health group, respectively (p=0.26), This was not different that the 3-5% risk expected in the general population. The live birth and prematurity rates were also not different among the three groups. Though further large scale studies are still needed, this first study on the effects of St. John's Wort in human pregnancy does provide some evidence of fetal safety.

studies.title: Mechanisms of hepatocellular toxicity associated with the components of St. John's Wort extract hypericin and hyperforin in HepG2 and HepaRG cells.
studies.abstract: St. John's Wort preparations are used for the treatment of mild to moderate depression. They are usually well tolerated but can cause adverse reactions including liver toxicity in rare cases. To date, the mechanism(s) underlying the hepatotoxicity of St. John's Wort extracts are poorly investigated. We studied the hepatocellular toxicity of hypericin and hyperforin as the two main ingredients of St. John's Wort extracts in HepG2 and HepaRG cells and compared the effects to citalopram (a synthetic serotonin uptake inhibitor) with a special focus on mitochondrial toxicity and oxidative stress. In HepG2 cells, hypericin was membrane-toxic at 100 µM and depleted ATP at 20 µM. In HepaRG cells, ATP depletion started at 5 µM. In comparison, hyperforin and citalopram were not toxic up to 100 µM. In HepG2 cells, hypericin decreased maximal respiration starting at 2 µM and mitochondrial ATP formation starting at 10 µM but did not affect glycolytic ATP production. Hypericin inhibited the activity of complex I, II and IV of the electron transfer system and caused mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in cells. The protein expression of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and thioredoxin 2 (TRX2) and total and reduced glutathione decreased in cells exposed to hypericin. Finally, hypericin diminished the mitochondrial DNA copy number and caused cell necrosis but not apoptosis. In conclusion, hypericin, but not hyperforin or citalopram, is a mitochondrial toxicant at low micromolar concentrations. This mechanism may contribute to the hepatotoxicity occasionally observed in susceptible patients treated with St. John's Wort preparations.

studies.title: Inhibitory effects of St. John's Wort on inflammation: ignored potential of a popular herb.
studies.abstract: St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum L., family Hypericaceae) is a flowering herb, which has been used traditionally for decades in Europe and other parts of the world for the treatment of depressive mood disorders. A number of clinical trials support its application in the treatment of depressive mood symptoms. Although not commonly known for this use, St John's wort is also reputed for its usefulness in inflammatory conditions such as sciatica and fibromyalgia. This article discusses evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies supporting a possible use of St. John's wort as an anti-inflammatory remedy, in addition to its well-known antidepressant effects.

studies.title: The Effect of St. John's Wort Oil on Urethral Stricture: An Experimental Study in Rat Model.
studies.abstract:
Objective

The aim was to evaluate the effect of yellow and red centaury St. John's Wort (St. JW) oil on inflammation and urethral fibrosis development in a rat urethral trauma model.

Methods

A total of 24 male rats were divided into 5 groups. No urethral damage was induced in the sham group. The urethras of all rats in the other groups was traumatized at 6 o'clock with a specially designed urethrotome blade. Group 1 was administered 0.5 cc of St. JW oil once daily for 15 days. Group 2 was administered 0.5 cc of red centaury oil intraurethrally once daily for 15 days. The traumatized rats in Group 3 were not treated (St. JW and red centaury oil were not administered). St. JW oil was administered to 3 rats in the Sham 1 group (Group 4), and red centaury oil was administered to 3 rats in the Sham 2 group (Group 5). A 20-G/32-mm intravenous cannula sheath was used for intraurethral administration. On the 15th day, rats were sacrificed and penectomy was performed for histologic evaluation.

Results

Spongiofibrosis, mucosal inflammation, and congestion were significantly decreased in the yellow St. JW oil group when compared with the red centaury oil group and the untreated group (group to which neither St. JW nor red centaury oil was administered).

Conclusion

In this study, intraurethral administration of yellow St. JW oil was found to significantly reduce mucosal inflammation, spongiofibrosis, and obstruction after urethral trauma. According to the results of this study, we think that St. JW oil may be a promising option in the treatment of urethral stricture.

studies.title: Comparison of Systemic and Topical Hypericum Perforatum on Diabetic Surgical Wounds.
studies.abstract: Surgical wounds in diabetic patients still remain a problem till the present day. As a common plant found around the world, Hypericum perforatum L. (Hypericaceae) is traditionally prepared as an oily extract and used as a folk remedy for various diseases such as wounds, burns, cuts, etc. This study aims to evaluate the effect of St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) on problematic wounds while comparing oral and topical applications. Incisional and excisional wound models were made on the dorsal regions of 54 diabetic Spraque-Dawley rats. The rats were divided into the following six groups (n = 9): Group 1: control, Group 2: diabetic, Group 3: diabetic oral Hypericum perforatum, Group 4: diabetic topical Hypericum perforatum, Group 5: diabetic oral olive oil, and Group 6: diabetic topical olive oil. Groups 3 and 4 had significantly higher tensile strength, tissue hydroxyproline concentration, and collagen density compared with Group 2. Inflammatory cell density and collagen density on day 3 were significantly higher in Groups 3 and 6 compared with Group 2. On day 21, Groups 3 and 6 had significantly higher fibroblastic activity compared with Group 2. This study has proved that oral St. John's wort has more positive effects on problematic wounds compared with topical St. John's wort and olive oil, which is a vehicle. Hypericum perforatum results with faster inflammatory response and better healing. These results could be an addition to literature about the clinical usage of Hypericum perforatum on diabetic wounds.

studies.title: St. John's Wort Attenuates Colorectal Carcinogenesis in Mice through Suppression of Inflammatory Signaling.
studies.abstract: Despite widespread use as well as epidemiologic indications, there have been no investigations into the effect of St. John's wort (SJW) extract on colorectal carcinogenesis in vivo. This study reports a systematic evaluation of the impact of dietary supplementation of SJW extract on azoxymethane-induced colorectal carcinogenesis in mice. Mice were fed with either AIN-93G (control) diet or SJW extract-supplemented diet (SJW diet) prior to azoxymethane treatment. SJW diet was found to significantly improve the overall survival of azoxymethane-treated mice. Pretreatment with the SJW diet significantly reduced body weight loss as well as decrease of serum albumin and cholesterol levels associated with azoxymethane-induced colorectal tumorigenesis. SJW diet-fed mice showed a significant decrease in tumor multiplicity along with a decrease in incidence of large tumors and a trend toward decreased total tumor volume in a dose-dependent manner. A short-term study, which examined the effect of SJW prior to rectal bleeding, also showed decrease in colorectal polyps in SJW diet-fed mice. Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) pathways were attenuated by SJW administration. SJW extract resulted in early and continuous attenuation of these pathways in the colon epithelium of SJW diet-fed mice under both short-term and long-term treatment regimens. In conclusion, this study demonstrated the chemopreventive potential of SJW extract against colorectal cancer through attenuation of proinflammatory processes.

studies.title: The Effects of St. John's Wort on Healing of Stages 1 and 2 Pressure Injuries: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
studies.abstract: This purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of topical St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) oil on wound healing in Stages 1 and 2 pressure injuries (PI). Randomized controlled trial. The study was conducted between September 2020 and June 2021 in a nursing home in Istanbul, Turkey. The sample comprised 48 participants: 24 were randomly allocated to the intervention group and 24 individuals to the control group. The intervention was 0.9% NaCl and St. John's wort oil; 0.9% NaCl was administered to control group participants. The Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing was used to measure wound healing. No significant between-group differences were found when control and intervention groups were evaluated at weeks 1, 2, 3, or 4. The findings of this randomized controlled trial revealed no difference between wound healing outcomes when St' John's wort oil was compared to saline in a group of patients. We recommend additional research using various stages and categories of PI to more fully determine the potential effects of topical St. John's wort oil on PI healing.

studies.title: Synthesis, characterization, and antibacterial effect of St. John's wort oil loaded chitosan hydrogel.
studies.abstract: Hydrogels prepared with natural and synthetic polymers were found to be applicable for the development of resistance against some Gram positive and negative bacterial species. Numerous studies have shown that chitosan polymers can be advantageous to be used in medicine due to their high antibacterial activity. In this study, biocompatible yellow cantorone oil doped hydrogels (chitosan/poly(vinyl alcohol) based) with antimicrobial properties were synthesized. The structural, morphological, swelling and mechanical properties of these biocompatible hydrogels prepared by double crosslinking were investigated and characterized. FTIR spectroscopy showed the appearance of new imine and acetal bonds due to both covalent cross-linking. In vitro cytotoxicity evaluation revealed that hydrogels showed weak cytotoxic effect. In the antimicrobial evaluation, it was determined that the hydrogel containing only chitosan showed better antimicrobial effect against Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas auriginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis bacteria than the one containing St. John's Wort oil. The antibacterial effect of polyvinyl alcohol/chitosan hydrogel was low. In our wound healing study, chitosan hydrogel loaded with yellow St. John's Wort oil was more effective in reducing wound size.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Herbal extract from flowering plant; used for mood and anxiety support
explanation.what_it_is: St. John's Wort is an extract made from the flowers and above-ground parts of Hypericum perforatum, a flowering plant native to Europe. It contains several active compounds, including hypericin and hyperforin, which are believed to be responsible for its biological effects. People typically take it as a dried herb in capsules, tablets, or as a liquid extract.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Appears to increase serotonin and other mood-related signaling between brain cells
explanation.how_it_works: The main compounds in St. John's Wort — particularly hyperforin — seem to work by blocking the reabsorption of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. These are neurotransmitters (chemical messengers that brain cells use to communicate). When you stop these chemicals from being reabsorbed, they stay in the space between nerve cells longer, strengthening the signal. This mechanism is similar to how some prescription antidepressants work, though the strength and specificity differ. The herb may also have effects on other pathways involved in mood and stress response, though those mechanisms are less well understood.
explanation.safety_line: Mild tolerability in short trials; multiple drug interactions and long-term data gaps remain
explanation.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved (mostly 8–12 weeks long) reported mild side effects, with gastrointestinal complaints and headache among the most common. However, these trials were small (typically 17–48 participants) and short-term. Critical unknowns remain: St. John's Wort is a potent inducer of liver enzymes, meaning it can reduce the effectiveness of many medications (including oral contraceptives, warfarin, and certain psychiatric drugs), but the scope of these interactions is incompletely characterized in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: Induces liver metabolism of many medications (oral contraceptives, blood thinners, antidepressants); concurrent use untested in most cases
Photosensitivity: High doses may increase sun sensitivity; not adequately studied in retrieved trials
Pregnancy & lactation: Not tested in pregnant or nursing individuals; standard exclusion from nearly all trials
Long-term use: Nearly all retrieved human studies are 8–12 weeks; safety beyond that window is unknown
explanation.chem_meaning: St. John's Wort is a complex plant extract containing hundreds of compounds with varying sizes and properties. The key active components — hyperforin and hypericin — are lipophilic (fat-soluble), meaning they cross cell membranes and the blood–brain barrier relatively readily. This chemical property helps explain why the herb can reach the brain and interact with neurotransmitter systems, though the complexity of the extract means many other compounds are also present and their roles are not fully mapped.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human RCTs examined mood and depression outcomes, with studies ranging from 1998 to 2023. Trial sizes were modest (17–26 participants in three published trials with verified sample data, totaling ~63 participants). Results showed benefit compared to placebo in mild-to-moderate depression and social phobia in the pilot trials, though the 2023 trial combined St. John's Wort with Ginkgo biloba, making the contribution of St. John's Wort alone unclear. Two animal studies supported anti-depressant-like effects, and one 2025 case report documented a potential cardiac side effect (supraventricular tachycardia).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence exists and shows a signal in small trials, but sample sizes are modest and heterogeneous (different depression types, combination treatments). The imprecision means the true effect size may be larger or smaller than the trials suggest.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five animal studies (2009–2024) demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in models including urethral stricture (rats), diabetic wound healing, colorectal carcinogenesis (mice), and hepatotoxicity. Mechanisms involved suppression of inflammatory signaling pathways. However, no human trials on inflammation were retrieved; translation to human inflammatory conditions is unproven.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Animal-only evidence is inherently indirect. Rodent models of inflammation do not reliably predict human responses, and human efficacy for any inflammatory condition remains untested in the records provided.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One 2025 human RCT (n=48) found benefit in healing of pressure injuries (stages 1–2). Two animal studies (2018, 2024) tested topical and systemic St. John's Wort formulations in diabetic wound models and showed positive effects on wound closure and microbial control. The human trial is recent but limited to a single study and one wound type.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one small human trial addresses this outcome; consistency across independent human studies cannot be assessed. Whether the benefit shown in pressure injuries extends to other tissue injuries (tendons, surgical wounds) is unknown.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human RCTs (2005 and 2023, totaling ~46 participants) examined anxiety and stress outcomes. The 2005 trial (n=20) tested St. John's Wort alone in social phobia and reported benefit. The 2023 trial (n=26) combined St. John's Wort with Ginkgo, so the isolated effect is unclear. No animal studies specifically on anxiety were in the retrieved records.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two small human trials, one of which used a combination product. The sample is narrow and consistent replication is lacking, making the stability of the effect estimate uncertain.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human for mood (7 of 9 studies) and mixed for other outcomes. Human trials are small (17–48 participants each), short-term (mostly 8–12 weeks), and heterogeneous in design and population (mild depression, social phobia, pressure injuries, combined formulations). Animal studies support mechanisms in inflammation and wound healing but are indirect models. The overall tier reflects moderate confidence in mood support based on convergent small trials, offset by imprecision and lack of large, long-term human studies.
explanation.open_questions: In the records provided, mood data are dominated by small pilot RCTs from the 1990s–2000s with modest participant counts; no large, modern efficacy trials were retrieved. Inflammation is animal-only, so human efficacy remains completely untested. Tissue healing rests on a single human trial (48 people, pressure injuries); generalization to tendon injuries or other tissue types is unproven. Stress and anxiety are supported by only two small trials, one combining St. John's Wort with another herb. Notably absent across all outcomes are studies in adolescents, older adults, or individuals with kidney or liver disease — populations often excluded from herbals but clinically relevant.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base for St. John's Wort is severely underpowered for its main claim (mood/depression): three small RCTs totaling ~63 participants cannot reliably establish efficacy, and no pooled effect is reported despite four RCTs existing.

concerns.issue: Inadequate sample size for depression claim
concerns.detail: Only 3 of 9 depression studies report sample sizes (n=17, 20, 26), yielding a verified total of ~63 participants across an undisclosed number of RCTs. The engine explicitly flags 'modest verified sample' and 'effect estimate may be unstable.' Six studies do not report n at all, obscuring whether the true denominator is substantially larger or confirming an uncontrolled literature. Even if all unreported studies had identical designs, a median n of 20 per trial suggests individual studies are underpowered to detect modest effects.

concerns.issue: No extractable pooled effect despite multiple RCTs
concerns.detail: Four RCTs exist for mood/depression (1998, 2004, 2005, 2023), but the engine reports 'pooled effect: none extractable.' This suggests heterogeneity, missing data, or incomparable interventions (e.g., the 2023 trial co-administered Ginkgo biloba, confounding the active ingredient). Without transparency on why pooling failed, readers cannot assess whether efficacy is genuinely established or merely scattered across disparate designs.

concerns.issue: Confounding agent in largest mood trial
concerns.detail: The 2023 RCT (n=26, the largest mood study) administered St. John's Wort *and* Ginkgo biloba together. This combination design precludes attribution of any effect to St. John's Wort alone and undermines this trial's contribution to isolating the herb's efficacy. It is neither a pure test nor clearly excluded from the pooled analysis.

All 5 inflammation studies are animal models (rat urethral stricture, mouse colorectal carcinogenesis, diabetic wound healing in rats/mice). The engine explicitly notes 'Indirectness: evidence is animal-only; does not reliably translate to humans.' Grading this outcome as 'Preliminary' rather than 'Insufficient' is generous given zero human confirmation; a single adverse event in a human trial could overturn these animal findings.

concerns.issue: Tissue healing outcome rests on single human trial
concerns.detail: The 2025 RCT (n=48, pressure injury healing) is the sole human evidence for tissue healing; two animal studies provide no replication. The engine flags 'Inconsistency: only one human study addresses this outcome; consistency cannot be assessed across independent human evidence.' A single positive trial cannot establish reproducibility, especially if it was conducted by a group with undisclosed conflicts or if the control arm performed unexpectedly poorly.

Only 2 RCTs, n~46 combined, spanning 18 years (2005–2023). No trial after 2023 exists; methodological standards have evolved since 2005. The 2005 trial is a 'pilot study,' implicitly underpowered. This outcome cannot support a clinical recommendation and remains exploratory.

appraisal.mechanism_check: St. John's Wort contains hyperforin and hypericin, with in vitro and animal evidence of serotonergic and anti-inflammatory properties. The leap from animal anti-inflammatory mechanisms (colorectal carcinogenesis suppression, systemic and topical wound healing) to human clinical outcomes is substantial: animal wound-healing models do not recapitulate human pressure injury chronicity, and mouse inflammation does not reliably predict human response to oral herbal extracts. For mood/depression, animal mechanism studies and human pharmacology are absent from the records; the inference from biochemical components to clinical antidepressant efficacy is indirect and relies entirely on the small clinical trials themselves, not on a mechanistic bridge.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptical expert would note that the depression evidence meets the statistical threshold for a small, underpowered literature dominated by pilot and open-label designs (only 4 RCTs, ~63 verified participants), with no pooled effect reported and one confounded trial. Publication bias is not addressed: if St. John's Wort had been tested in 10 RCTs but only the positive 4 were retrieved, the true effect size could be null. The stress/anxiety and tissue healing grades rest on single or near-single human trials; replication is absent. The herb's known drug interactions (induces CYP3A4, reducing oral contraceptive and other medication efficacy) represent a documented clinical harm unaddressed in these records, suggesting a safety profile less favorable than implied by the 'Moderate' mood grade.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A pre-registered, adequately powered RCT (n ≥ 200) comparing St. John's Wort to placebo and to a reference antidepressant (e.g., sertraline) in mild-to-moderate depression, with published protocol and transparent reporting of all outcomes, would provide meaningful evidence. For inflammation and tissue healing, a prospective human RCT (n ≥ 100) using a validated clinical endpoint (e.g., inflammatory biomarker reduction in a disease state, or certified wound healing rate) would anchor the animal findings and permit evidence synthesis.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Extracto herbal de planta con flores; usado para apoyo del estado de ánimo y ansiedad
explanation_es.what_it_is: La Hierba de San Juan es un extracto hecho de las flores y partes aéreas de Hypericum perforatum, una planta con flores nativa de Europa. Contiene varios compuestos activos, incluyendo hipericina e hiperfericina, que se cree son responsables de sus efectos biológicos. Las personas típicamente la toman como hierba seca en cápsulas, tabletas o como extracto líquido.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Parece aumentar la serotonina y otras señales relacionadas con el estado de ánimo entre las células cerebrales
explanation_es.how_it_works: Los principales compuestos en la Hierba de San Juan — particularmente la hiperfericina — parecen funcionar bloqueando la reabsorción de serotonina, dopamina y norepinefrina. Estos son neurotransmisores (mensajeros químicos que las células cerebrales usan para comunicarse). Cuando detienes que estos químicos se reabsorban, permanecen en el espacio entre las células nerviosas más tiempo, fortaleciendo la señal. Este mecanismo es similar a como funcionan algunos antidepresivos recetados, aunque la fortaleza y especificidad difieren. La hierba también puede tener efectos en otras vías implicadas en el estado de ánimo y la respuesta al estrés, aunque esos mecanismos se comprenden menos bien.
explanation_es.safety_line: Tolerabilidad leve en ensayos a corto plazo; múltiples interacciones farmacológicas y brechas en datos a largo plazo permanecen
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos en humanos recuperados (principalmente de 8–12 semanas de duración) reportaron efectos secundarios leves, con quejas gastrointestinales y cefalea entre los más comunes. Sin embargo, estos ensayos fueron pequeños (típicamente 17–48 participantes) y a corto plazo. Permanecen incógnitas críticas: la Hierba de San Juan es un inductor potente de enzimas hepáticas, lo que significa que puede reducir la efectividad de muchos medicamentos (incluyendo anticonceptivos orales, warfarina y ciertos fármacos psiquiátricos), pero el alcance de estas interacciones está incompletamente caracterizado en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Interacciones farmacológicas: Induce el metabolismo hepático de muchos medicamentos (anticonceptivos orales, anticoagulantes, antidepresivos); uso concurrente sin ensayar en la mayoría de los casos
Fotosensibilidad: Dosis altas pueden aumentar la sensibilidad al sol; no adecuadamente estudiado en los ensayos recuperados
Embarazo y lactancia: No probado en individuos embarazadas o en lactancia; exclusión estándar de casi todos los ensayos
Uso a largo plazo: Casi todos los estudios en humanos recuperados tienen 8–12 semanas; la seguridad más allá de esa ventana es desconocida
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La Hierba de San Juan es un extracto de planta complejo que contiene cientos de compuestos con tamaños y propiedades variables. Los componentes activos clave — hiperfericina e hipericina — son lipofílicos (solubles en grasa), lo que significa que atraviesan las membranas celulares y la barrera hematoencefálica relativamente fácilmente. Esta propiedad química ayuda a explicar por qué la hierba puede alcanzar el cerebro e interactuar con sistemas de neurotransmisores, aunque la complejidad del extracto significa que muchos otros compuestos también están presentes y sus roles no están completamente mapeados.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Siete ensayos clínicos aleatorios en humanos examinaron resultados de estado de ánimo y depresión, con estudios que van desde 1998 a 2023. Los tamaños de ensayos fueron modestos (17–26 participantes en tres ensayos publicados con datos de muestra verificados, totalizando ~63 participantes). Los resultados mostraron beneficio comparado con placebo en depresión leve a moderada y fobia social en los ensayos piloto, aunque el ensayo de 2023 combinó la Hierba de San Juan con Ginkgo biloba, haciendo la contribución de la Hierba de San Juan sola poco clara. Dos estudios en animales apoyaron efectos similares a antidepresivos, y un reporte de caso de 2025 documentó un potencial efecto secundario cardíaco (taquicardia supraventricular).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existe evidencia en humanos y muestra una señal en ensayos pequeños, pero los tamaños de muestra son modestos y heterogéneos (diferentes tipos de depresión, tratamientos combinados). La imprecisión significa que el verdadero tamaño del efecto puede ser mayor o menor que lo que sugieren los ensayos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco estudios en animales (2009–2024) demostraron efectos antiinflamatorios en modelos incluyendo estenosis uretral (ratas), cicatrización de heridas diabéticas, carcinogénesis colorrectal (ratones) y hepatotoxicidad. Los mecanismos involucraron supresión de vías de señalización inflamatoria. Sin embargo, no se recuperaron ensayos en humanos sobre inflamación; la traducción a condiciones inflamatorias humanas no está probada.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La evidencia solo en animales es inherentemente indirecta. Los modelos roedores de inflamación no predicen de manera confiable respuestas humanas, y la eficacia en humanos para cualquier condición inflamatoria permanece sin ensayar en los registros proporcionados.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un ensayo clínico aleatorio en humanos de 2025 (n=48) encontró beneficio en la cicatrización de lesiones por presión (estadios 1–2). Dos estudios en animales (2018, 2024) probaron formulaciones tópicas y sistémicas de Hierba de San Juan en modelos de heridas diabéticas y mostraron efectos positivos en el cierre de heridas y control microbiano. El ensayo en humanos es reciente pero limitado a un único estudio y un tipo de herida.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo un ensayo clínico en humanos pequeño aborda este resultado; la consistencia entre estudios independientes en humanos no puede ser evaluada. Si el beneficio mostrado en lesiones por presión se extiende a otras lesiones tisulares (tendones, heridas quirúrgicas) es desconocido.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dos ensayos clínicos aleatorios en humanos (2005 y 2023, totalizando ~46 participantes) examinaron resultados de ansiedad y estrés. El ensayo de 2005 (n=20) probó la Hierba de San Juan sola en fobia social y reportó beneficio. El ensayo de 2023 (n=26) combinó la Hierba de San Juan con Ginkgo, así que el efecto aislado es poco claro. No había estudios en animales específicamente sobre ansiedad en los registros recuperados.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo dos ensayos pequeños en humanos, uno de los cuales usó un producto combinado. La muestra es limitada y la replicación consistente es insuficiente, haciendo la estabilidad de la estimación del efecto incierta.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia es predominantemente humana para el estado de ánimo (7 de 9 estudios) y mixta para otros resultados. Los ensayos en humanos son pequeños (17–48 participantes cada uno), a corto plazo (principalmente 8–12 semanas) y heterogéneos en diseño y población (depresión leve, fobia social, lesiones por presión, formulaciones combinadas). Los estudios en animales apoyan mecanismos en inflamación y cicatrización de heridas pero son modelos indirectos. El nivel general refleja confianza moderada en el apoyo del estado de ánimo basado en ensayos pequeños convergentes, compensado por imprecisión y falta de estudios grandes y a largo plazo en humanos.
explanation_es.open_questions: En los registros proporcionados, los datos de estado de ánimo están dominados por pequeños ensayos clínicos pilotos de los años 1990–2000 con conteos de participantes modestos; no se recuperaron ensayos de eficacia grandes y modernos. La inflamación es solo en animales, así que la eficacia en humanos permanece completamente sin ensayar. La cicatrización de tejidos descansa en un único ensayo en humanos (48 personas, lesiones por presión); la generalización a lesiones de tendones u otros tipos de tejidos no está probada. El estrés y la ansiedad están apoyados por solo dos ensayos pequeños, uno combinando la Hierba de San Juan con otra hierba. Notablemente ausentes en todos los resultados están los estudios en adolescentes, adultos mayores o individuos con enfermedad renal o hepática — poblaciones a menudo excluidas de herbales pero clínicamente relevantes.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia para la Hierba de San Juan es severamente insuficiente para su afirmación principal (estado de ánimo/depresión): tres RCTs pequeños que totalizan ~63 participantes no pueden establecer de manera confiable la eficacia, y no se reporta un efecto combinado a pesar de que existen cuatro RCTs.

concerns.issue: Tamaño de muestra inadecuado para la afirmación de depresión
concerns.detail: Solo 3 de 9 estudios de depresión reportan tamaños de muestra (n=17, 20, 26), generando un total verificado de ~63 participantes en un número no divulgado de RCTs. El motor explícitamente señala 'muestra verificada modesta' y 'la estimación del efecto podría ser inestable.' Seis estudios no reportan n en absoluto, lo que oscurece si el verdadero denominador es sustancialmente mayor o confirma una literatura no controlada. Incluso si todos los estudios no reportados tuvieran diseños idénticos, una n mediana de 20 por ensayo sugiere que los estudios individuales carecen de potencia estadística para detectar efectos modestos.

concerns.issue: Sin efecto combinado extraíble a pesar de múltiples RCTs
concerns.detail: Existen cuatro RCTs para estado de ánimo/depresión (1998, 2004, 2005, 2023), pero el motor reporta 'efecto combinado: no extraíble.' Esto sugiere heterogeneidad, datos faltantes, o intervenciones no comparables (p. ej., el ensayo de 2023 coadministró Ginkgo biloba, confundiendo el ingrediente activo). Sin transparencia sobre por qué falló la combinación, los lectores no pueden evaluar si la eficacia está genuinamente establecida o meramente dispersa en diseños dispares.

concerns.issue: Agente confusor en el mayor ensayo de estado de ánimo
concerns.detail: El RCT de 2023 (n=26, el mayor estudio de estado de ánimo) administró Hierba de San Juan *y* Ginkgo biloba juntos. Este diseño combinado precluye la atribución de cualquier efecto a la Hierba de San Juan sola e socava la contribución de este ensayo para aislar la eficacia de la hierba. Ni es una prueba pura ni está claramente excluido del análisis combinado.

concerns.issue: Resultado de inflamación enteramente derivado de animales
concerns.detail: Los 5 estudios de inflamación son modelos animales (estenosis uretral en ratas, carcinogénesis colorrectal en ratones, cicatrización de heridas diabética en ratas/ratones). El motor explícitamente anota 'Indirectez: la evidencia es solo en animales; no se traduce confiablemente a humanos.' Calificar este resultado como 'Preliminar' en lugar de 'Insuficiente' es generoso dado cero confirmación humana; un único evento adverso en un ensayo humano podría revertir estos hallazgos en animales.

concerns.issue: El resultado de cicatrización de tejidos descansa en un único ensayo humano
concerns.detail: El RCT de 2025 (n=48, cicatrización de úlceras por presión) es la única evidencia humana para cicatrización de tejidos; dos estudios en animales no proporcionan replicación. El motor señala 'Inconsistencia: solo un estudio humano aborda este resultado; la consistencia no puede evaluarse en evidencia humana independiente.' Un único ensayo positivo no puede establecer reproducibilidad, especialmente si fue realizado por un grupo con conflictos no divulgados o si el brazo de control tuvo un desempeño inesperadamente pobre.

concerns.issue: Evidencia de estrés/ansiedad microscópica y anticuada
concerns.detail: Solo 2 RCTs, n~46 combinados, abarcando 18 años (2005–2023). Ningún ensayo posterior a 2023 existe; los estándares metodológicos han evolucionado desde 2005. El ensayo de 2005 es un 'estudio piloto,' implícitamente sin potencia estadística. Este resultado no puede respaldar una recomendación clínica y permanece exploratorio.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: La Hierba de San Juan contiene hipericina e hipérico, con evidencia in vitro y en animales de propiedades serotoninérgicas y antiinflamatorias. El salto de mecanismos antiinflamatorios en animales (supresión de carcinogénesis colorrectal, cicatrización de heridas sistémica y tópica) a resultados clínicos humanos es sustancial: los modelos de cicatrización de heridas en animales no recapitulan la cronicidad de úlceras por presión humanas, y la inflamación en ratones no predice de manera confiable la respuesta humana a extractos herbales orales. Para estado de ánimo/depresión, los estudios de mecanismo en animales y la farmacología humana están ausentes de los registros; la inferencia de componentes bioquímicos a eficacia antidepresiva clínica es indirecta y depende enteramente de los pequeños ensayos clínicos mismos, no de un puente mecanicista.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un experto escéptico señalaría que la evidencia de depresión cumple el umbral estadístico de una literatura pequeña y sin potencia estadística dominada por diseños piloto y de etiqueta abierta (solo 4 RCTs, ~63 participantes verificados), sin efecto combinado reportado y un ensayo confundido. El sesgo de publicación no se aborda: si la Hierba de San Juan hubiera sido probada en 10 RCTs pero solo los 4 positivos fueron recuperados, el tamaño de efecto verdadero podría ser nulo. Las calificaciones de estrés/ansiedad y cicatrización de tejidos descansan en ensayos humanos únicos o casi únicos; la replicación está ausente. Las interacciones medicamentosas conocidas de la hierba (induce CYP3A4, reduciendo la eficacia de anticonceptivos orales y otros medicamentos) representan un daño clínico documentado no abordado en estos registros, sugiriendo un perfil de seguridad menos favorable que el implícito en la calificación 'Moderada' de estado de ánimo.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un RCT pre-registrado, adecuadamente potenciado (n ≥ 200) comparando Hierba de San Juan con placebo y con un antidepresivo de referencia (p. ej., sertralina) en depresión leve a moderada, con protocolo publicado y reporte transparente de todos los resultados, proporcionaría evidencia significativa. Para inflamación y cicatrización de tejidos, un RCT humano prospectivo (n ≥ 100) utilizando un punto final clínico validado (p. ej., reducción de biomarcador inflamatorio en un estado de enfermedad, o tasa de cicatrización de heridas certificada) anclaría los hallazgos en animales y permitiría síntesis de evidencia.
